q: What was Gautama Buddha’s early name as a prince? [JAC PYQ]
o: Rahula
Vivekananda
Siddhartha Gautama
Ashoka Maurya
e: Gautama Buddha began his life as a prince named Siddhartha Gautama (563 B.C.–483 B.C.) in northern India.

q: Who adapted/wrote the prose lesson "The Sermon at Benares" in First Flight?
o: Vallikkannan
Lucio Rodrigues
Albert Einstein
Betty Renshaw
e: The textbook lesson "The Sermon at Benares" is credited to Betty Renshaw (adapted from Values and Voices: A College Reader).

q: At what age was Prince Siddhartha sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures?
o: Ten years
Twelve years
Sixteen years
Twenty-five years
e: At twelve, he was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures, returning home four years later.

q: Four years after going away for schooling at twelve, what happened in Siddhartha’s life?
o: He became a potter
He became a wandering beggar
He returned home to marry a princess
He went straight to Benares
e: Four years after leaving at twelve, Siddhartha returned home and married a princess.

q: For how many years did Siddhartha and his princess live "as befitted royalty" after having a son?
o: Ten years
Twenty years
Five years
Seven years
e: They had a son and lived for ten years in royal comfort before he stepped out at about twenty-five.

q: At about what age did Prince Siddhartha first encounter the sufferings of the world while out hunting?
o: Twenty-five
Thirty
Forty
Eighteen
e: At about the age of twenty-five, the Prince, previously shielded from suffering, saw the four sights while out hunting.

q: Which four sights moved Siddhartha to leave his palace in search of enlightenment?
o: A king, a soldier, a merchant, and a farmer
A sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and a monk begging for alms
A river, a mountain, a boat, and a palace
A potter, a gardener, an ox, and a fruit
e: Seeing a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and a begging monk moved Siddhartha to seek enlightenment.

q: For how many years did Siddhartha wander before sitting down under the peepal tree?
o: Ten years
Three years
Five years
Seven years
e: He wandered for seven years and finally sat down under a peepal tree, vowing to stay until enlightenment came.

q: After how many days under the peepal tree did Siddhartha attain enlightenment?
o: Seven days
Forty days
One day
Three days
e: Enlightened after seven days, he renamed the peepal tree the Bodhi Tree (Tree of Wisdom).

q: What did Siddhartha rename the peepal tree after attaining enlightenment beneath it?
o: Bodhi Tree (Tree of Wisdom)
Ashoka Tree
Banyan of Peace
Kalpavriksha
e: He renamed the peepal tree the Bodhi Tree, meaning the Tree of Wisdom.

q: What does the title "the Buddha" literally mean in the lesson?
o: The Mighty Ruler
The Awakened or the Enlightened
The Great Warrior
The Wealthy Merchant
e: Once he began teaching after his enlightenment, he became known as the Buddha ("the Awakened or the Enlightened").

q: Where did Gautama Buddha preach his first sermon? [JAC PYQ]
o: Delhi
Bodh Gaya
Kapilavastu
Benares
e: NCERT states explicitly that the Buddha preached his first sermon at the city of Benares, on the River Ganges.

q: Benares is described in the chapter as the holiest of the dipping places on which river?
o: River Ganges
River Narmada
River Yamuna
River Saraswati
e: Benares is introduced as the "most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges."

q: Who had died in Kisa Gotami’s family, plunging her into deep grief?
o: Her only son
Her father
Her younger sister
Her husband
e: Kisa Gotami had an only son, and he died; in her grief she carried the dead child around seeking medicine.

q: What did Kisa Gotami ask all her neighbours for when carrying her dead child?
o: Food
Medicine
Mustard-seed
Money
e: Carrying her dead child to all her neighbours, she begged them for medicine to cure him.

q: Whom did a man advise Kisa Gotami to visit as a "physician" who could help her?
o: The town potter
Sakyamuni, the Buddha
The village herbalist
The king of Kapilavastu
e: The man directed her to Sakyamuni, the Buddha, saying he knew a physician who could help.

q: What did the Buddha ask Kisa Gotami to bring him before he could prepare the medicine?
o: A peepal leaf
An earthen vessel
A bowl of Ganges water
A handful of mustard-seed
e: The Buddha asked her to bring "a handful of mustard-seed," adding one crucial condition.

q: What strict condition did the Buddha attach to the handful of mustard-seed?
o: The seed must come from a house where no one has lost a child, husband, parent, or friend
The seeds must be grown by a monk
The seeds must cost nothing and be brought before sunrise
The seeds must come from a royal palace
e: The Buddha insisted the mustard-seed be taken from a house where no one had lost a child, husband, parent, or friend.

q: What reply did households give Kisa Gotami when she asked if anyone had died in their family?
o: "Nobody has ever died here"
"Alas! the living are few, but the dead are many. Do not remind us of our deepest grief."
"We never grow mustard-seed"
"Go and ask the king"
e: Every household had lost loved ones and replied, "Alas! the living are few, but the dead are many."

q: When Kisa Gotami became weary and hopeless, what did she sit at the wayside watching?
o: Soldiers marching past
Waves of the Ganges
The lights of the city flickering up and being extinguished again
Flocks of birds returning home
e: Sitting by the wayside, she watched the lights of the city flicker up and be extinguished again until darkness reigned.

q: Who is the poet of "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Carl Sandburg
Ogden Nash
W.B. Yeats (William Butler Yeats)
Robert Frost
e: The Irish poet W.B. Yeats wrote "For Anne Gregory."

q: What is the natural colour of Anne Gregory’s hair in the poem "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Dark brown
Yellow / honey-coloured
Snow white
Jet black
e: The speaker calls her hair "great honey-coloured / Ramparts at your ear" and repeatedly mentions her "yellow hair."

q: Which three hair-dye colours does Anne Gregory suggest setting in her hair?
o: Blue, green, or pink
Brown, or black, or carrot
Silver, gold, or grey
White, chestnut, or blonde
e: In stanza two, Anne says she can get a hair-dye to colour her hair "Brown, or black, or carrot."

q: In "For Anne Gregory", what does "great honey-coloured / Ramparts at your ear" refer to?
o: A yellow woollen scarf
Her golden earrings
Her thick honey-coloured hair falling around her ears
Stone walls around an Irish castle
e: The honey-coloured hair framing her ears is metaphorically compared to protective castle ramparts.

q: According to the third stanza of "For Anne Gregory", who declared he had found a text?
o: Anne Gregory’s father
A village potter
A desperate young man
An old religious man
e: The speaker says he heard "an old religious man / But yesternight declare / That he had found a text to prove..."

q: According to the old religious man’s text, who ALONE can love Anne Gregory for herself alone and not her yellow hair?
o: A desperate young suitor
Only God
Her childhood teacher
A loyal friend
e: The text proves "That only God, my dear, / Could love you for yourself alone / And not your yellow hair."

q: How many stanzas and total lines make up the poem "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Two stanzas, 10 lines
Three stanzas, 18 lines (6 lines per stanza)
Four stanzas, 16 lines
Five stanzas, 20 lines
e: The poem consists of three stanzas of six lines each, making eighteen lines in total.

q: Who is the speaker of the second stanza of "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Her mother
The poet / young speaker
Anne Gregory herself
The old religious man
e: Stanzas 1 and 3 are spoken by the speaker/poet, while stanza 2 is Anne Gregory’s reply ("But I can get a hair-dye...").

q: How can a person obtain peace of mind according to the Buddha in "The Sermon at Benares"? [JAC PYQ]
o: By collecting mustard-seeds in jars
By avoiding all human company
By weeping louder every day
By drawing out the arrow of lamentation, complaint, and grief and becoming composed
e: Buddha teaches that one who draws out the arrow of lamentation, complaint, and grief and becomes composed obtains peace of mind.

q: What does "But yesternight" mean in W.B. Yeats’s poem "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Just last night
Years ago in childhood
Early this morning
Tomorrow night
e: "Yesternight" is an archaic poetic word meaning "last night."

q: What did the neighbours say when Kisa Gotami carried her dead child asking for medicine?
o: "Take him to the king"
"She has lost her senses. The boy is dead."
"Give him warm milk"
"Wait till morning"
e: Seeing her ask for medicine for a dead child, people said, "She has lost her senses. The boy is dead."

q: How did Kisa Gotami react immediately upon hearing the Buddha’s request for mustard-seed, and how did her mood change later?
o: She bought seeds from a spice market
At first she was angry, then hopeful
At first she joyfully promised to procure it, but after visiting houses she grew weary and hopeless
She refused immediately and left
e: In her joy she first promised to procure it easily, but after hearing death’s universality in every house, she became weary and hopeless.

q: Watching the city lights flicker up and go out led Kisa Gotami to reflect on what truth?
o: That nobody lights lamps in winter
That she should move to another city
That city lamps used cheap oil
That human lives, like those lights, flicker up and are extinguished again, and death is common to all
e: She considered the fate of men—their lives flicker up and die out—and realised how selfish she had been in her grief.

q: What self-realisation did Kisa Gotami express to herself as darkness fell over the city?
o: "How selfish am I in my grief! Death is common to all; yet he who has surrendered all selfishness finds the path to immortality."
"My neighbours are cruel to refuse me"
"The city lights will burn forever"
"I will search fifty more villages"
e: She exclaimed, "How selfish am I in my grief! Death is common to all," recognising that surrendering selfishness leads to immortality.

q: Which two analogies does the Buddha use in his sermon to show that mortals are always subject to death?
o: Flowing rivers and drifting clouds
Ripe fruits (early in danger of falling) and earthen vessels made by the potter (ending in being broken)
Gold coins and iron swords
Green leaves and ocean pearls
e: He compares mortals to ripe fruits in constant danger of falling and earthen vessels made by a potter that all end in being broken.

q: Whom does the Buddha compare to "an ox that is led to the slaughter"?
o: Potters throwing clay
Prince Siddhartha’s hunting steed
Mortals carried off one by one by death while helpless relatives look on and lament
Farmers complaining of poor crops
e: He observes that while relatives look on lamenting deeply, mortals are carried off one by one like an ox led to the slaughter.

q: Why do "the wise do not grieve" according to the Buddha’s sermon?
o: Because they have no relatives
Because they live away from cities
Because they own great wealth
Because they know the terms of the world—that the world is afflicted with death and decay
e: Knowing the world is afflicted with death and decay, the wise understand the terms of the world and therefore do not grieve.

q: According to the Buddha, what happens to a person who continues weeping and grieving over the dead?
o: His pain becomes greater, his body suffers, and he makes himself sick and pale without saving the dead
He immediately attains peace of mind
His eyesight grows sharper
The dead are saved by his tears
e: Weeping neither saves the dead nor brings peace; instead, it increases pain, harms the body, and makes the mourner sick and pale.

q: What does the Buddha say applies equally to "both young and adult, both those who are fools and those who are wise"?
o: All reach the Bodhi Tree
All fall into the power of death; all are subject to death
All become wandering monks
All attain peace without effort
e: He states unequivocally that young and old, fools and wise alike fall into the power of death.

q: In the introductory paragraphs of "The Sermon at Benares", the Buddha’s first sermon is said to reflect his wisdom about what?
o: Agricultural harvests
Royal warfare tactics
One inscrutable kind of suffering
Rules of wealthy trade
e: The sermon has been preserved and "reflects the Buddha’s wisdom about one inscrutable kind of suffering."

q: Why does the speaker in stanza 1 of "For Anne Gregory" claim a young man can never love Anne for herself alone?
o: Because her family forbids marriage
Because she lives on an island
Because Anne refuses to talk to anyone
Because young men are thrown into despair by her striking "honey-coloured ramparts" (outer beauty)
e: Young men are captivated and thrown into despair by her glamorous honey-coloured hair rather than seeing her inner self.

q: Why does Anne Gregory propose dyeing her hair brown, black, or carrot?
o: To remove her alluring yellow colour so young men might love her for herself alone
To look older than her age
To hide from the old religious man
To prepare for a royal wedding
e: She wants to show that hair colour is temporary and external; changing it might encourage young men to love her for who she truly is.

q: How does the speaker respond in stanza 3 to Anne’s idea of dyeing her hair?
o: By arguing carrot-red hair is equally pretty
By citing an old religious man’s text proving that ONLY God can love her for herself alone, implying mortals remain swayed by looks
By claiming hair-dye harms the hair
By praising young men’s loyalty
e: He gently counters that human attraction still clings to appearance—according to a sacred text, only God loves a person solely for themselves.

q: Which sequence accurately traces Siddhartha Gautama’s early life in the chapter?
o: Meeting Kisa Gotami → schooling at 12 → sitting under peepal tree
Seven years wandering → schooling at 12 → four sights → marriage
Schooling at 12 → marriage & ten years of royalty → four sights at 25 → 7 years wandering → 7 days under Bodhi Tree
First sermon at Benares → four sights while hunting → marriage
e: The exact order is: schooling at 12, returning at 16 to marry & live 10 years as royalty, four sights at ~25, 7 years wandering, then 7 days under the peepal tree.

q: Why did the Buddha send Kisa Gotami from house to house asking for mustard-seed instead of lecturing her immediately?
o: To tire her out so she would sleep
To test which neighbour was richest
To inspect the village’s mustard harvest
So she would discover firsthand through lived experience that death touches every household, making acceptance internal rather than merely spoken
e: Overwhelmed by grief, she needed to discover death’s universality herself across every doorstep rather than simply hearing a lecture.

q: Which combination of sights made Siddhartha realize the existence of old age, disease, death, and the search for inner peace?
o: A sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and a monk begging for alms
A battlefield after war
A crowded river port
A royal banquet and dancers
e: Protected until then from worldly misery, these four encounters opened his eyes to sickness, ageing, death, and spiritual renunciation.

q: What exact reason drove Kisa Gotami to "repair to the Buddha" instead of performing funeral rites at first?
o: She disliked her neighbours
Refusing to accept death, she hunted for a cure and was directed by a stranger to Sakyamuni Buddha as a physician who could help
She wanted to see the Ganges
She hoped to buy rice
e: Unable to accept her only son’s death, she hunted for medicine until a stranger sent her to Sakyamuni Buddha as a "physician."

q: What does the Buddha teach about whether any born being can avoid dying?
o: Monks avoid death altogether
Kings escape death through prayer
There is no means by which those that have been born can avoid dying; after old age comes death
Only rich merchants live forever
e: The Buddha teaches clearly: "there is not any means by which those that have been born can avoid dying... of such a nature are living beings."

q: In stanza 1 of "For Anne Gregory", what does "Thrown into despair" convey about young men gazing at Anne?
o: They fail their studies
They become religious scholars
They hate her hairstyle
They become hopelessly smitten and frustrated with longing over her dazzling outward beauty
e: It conveys how deeply smitten and love-struck young men feel by her enchanting looks, reacting purely to her outer appearance.

q: Even if Anne dyes her hair brown, black, or carrot, who alone can love her unconditionally according to the poem’s conclusion?
o: Only God
Her childhood friends
Young poets in despair
The village elders
e: The concluding stanza affirms that unconditional love untainted by outward appearance belongs to God alone.

q: What helplessness of families does the Buddha point out when death arrives?
o: They cannot light city lamps
A father cannot save his son, nor can kinsmen save their relations
They cannot travel to Benares
They cannot speak to monks
e: He reminds listeners that a father cannot save his son, nor kinsmen their relations, when death takes them.

q: In "The Sermon at Benares", the Buddha’s advice not to grieve is rooted in what realisation?
o: Refusing to care for the living
Heartless indifference toward family
Wise acceptance of the inevitable terms of mortal existence so one finds composure and peace instead of self-harming despair
Mocking people who cry
e: Far from being cold, it represents wisdom: recognising mortality’s universal law to overcome futile suffering and gain peace.

q: Who is referred to as "Sakyamuni, the Buddha" in the lesson?
o: The king of Benares
The stranger Kisa Gotami met
Anne Gregory’s religious scholar
Gautama Buddha himself (Sage of the Sakyas)
e: "Sakyamuni" (Sage of the Sakya clan) refers directly to Gautama Buddha.

q: How would you describe the overall tone of Yeats’s poem "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Gentle, conversational, gently playful yet philosophically insightful
Dark and terrifying
Bitter political satire
Furious and aggressive
e: It reads like an affectionate, lightly playful dialogue ("my dear") that gently delivers a deep spiritual truth.

q: Who, according to the closing sentence of the Buddha’s sermon, becomes "free from sorrow, and be blessed"?
o: One who builds grand temples
One who has drawn out the arrow of grief, become composed, obtained peace, and overcome all sorrow
One who locks away all memories
One who refuses to meet neighbours
e: The final line concludes: he who draws out the arrow, becomes composed, and overcomes all sorrow becomes free from sorrow and blessed.

q: In "For Anne Gregory", what does Anne mean by setting "carrot" colour in her hair?
o: Bleaching hair pale white
Eating raw carrots for health
A bright orange-red shade of hair-dye
Braiding carrots into hair
e: Grouped with "brown" and "black," "carrot" playfully refers to a reddish-orange shade of hair-dye.

q: What shared human bond did Kisa Gotami encounter in every home across her search?
o: No one grew mustard-seed in Benares
Every family was wealthy royalty
Every family had never tasted sorrow
Every single home had lost a beloved member and carried deep grief beneath ordinary life
e: Literally no house existed where a beloved had not died, showing grief is a universal bond among all families.

q: What is the poetic effect of ending every stanza of "For Anne Gregory" with "...yourself alone / And not your yellow hair"?
o: It acts as a refrain emphasising the central contrast between inner self ("yourself alone") and outward beauty ("yellow hair")
It proves Anne never changed her mind
It shortens the poem’s narrative
It weakens the rhythm
e: Repeating those closing lines as a refrain anchors the central conflict across all three perspectives: young men, Anne, and God.

q: Did the Buddha actually intend to brew a physical potion from mustard-seeds to revive Kisa Gotami’s son?
o: Yes, he planned to brew an Ayurvedic medicine
No; it was a compassionate pedagogical method to help her discover the universality of death herself
Yes, if she had brought them before noon
No; he wanted to chase her out of town
e: Knowing no death-free household existed, the Buddha used this gentle task so she would discover truth through experience.

q: What metaphorical "arrow" must a seeker pull out to obtain peace of mind?
o: Memories of family names
An iron arrow shot in battle
The arrow of lamentation, and complaint, and grief
A wooden spear from hunting
e: Buddha uses a striking metaphor: "draw out the arrow of lamentation, and complaint, and grief."

q: Identify the principal poetic device used in the phrase "great honey-coloured / Ramparts at your ear" in "For Anne Gregory".
o: Oxymoron
Pun
Simile
Metaphor
e: Without using "like" or "as," her hair is directly called "ramparts" (fort walls), making it a clear metaphor.

q: What is the rhyme scheme of each six-line stanza in "For Anne Gregory"?
o: ABABCC
ABCBDB
ABCABC
AABBCC
e: Lines 2, 4, and 6 rhyme (despair/ear/hair; there/despair/hair; declare/dear/hair), giving each stanza an ABCBDB scheme.

q: What does the word "inscrutable" mean in the phrase "one inscrutable kind of suffering"?
o: Trivial and humorous
Mysterious; impossible to understand or interpret completely
Temporary and curable
Caused by poverty alone
e: "Inscrutable" means impossible to understand or fathom—describing the profound mystery of death and bereavement.

q: Which poetic device appears in "your yellow" (stanzas 1–3) and "Brown, or black" (stanza 2)?
o: Paradox
Pun
Alliteration
Personification
e: Repetition of initial consonant sounds (/y/ in "your yellow" and /b/ in "Brown, or black") is Alliteration.

q: In the sentence "Kisa Gotami repaired to the Buddha", what does the word "repaired" mean in context?
o: Returned home empty-handed
Argued loudly with
Fixed a broken roof
Went to (formal/archaic usage meaning proceeded toward)
e: In literary English, "repaired to" is a formal usage meaning "went to" or "made her way to."

q: What is the closest synonym for "lamentation" as used in the Buddha’s sermon?
o: Passionate expression of grief, weeping, and mourning
Strict financial planning
Silent prayer
Joyful celebration
e: "Lamentation" means an audible, passionate expression of deep grief and sorrow.

q: Which figure of speech is used in "As all earthen vessels made by the potter end in being broken, so is the life of mortals"?
o: Hyperbole
Simile / Analogy (explicit comparison using "As... so...")
Personification
Oxymoron
e: The explicit comparison introduced by "As... so..." draws a direct Simile (analogy) between fragile clay pots and mortal life.

q: In "the world is afflicted with death and decay", what does "afflicted with" mean?
o: Secretly rewarded with
Decorated joyfully with
Painfully affected or troubled by
Completely cured of
e: "Afflicted with" means distressed, troubled, or suffering severely from something.

q: What does "composed" mean in "become composed will obtain peace of mind"?
o: Deeply terrified
Exhausted from walking
Turned into music
Calm, serene, and having full control over one’s emotions
e: Used as an adjective here, "composed" means calm, collected, and in control of one’s feelings.

q: What does Kisa Gotami mean by calling earthly existence "this valley of desolation"?
o: The mortal world filled with sorrow, loss, and emptiness
A fertile tea valley
An abandoned forest shrine
A geographical canyon near Benares
e: "Valley of desolation" is a metaphor for the mortal world darkened by sorrow, bereavement, and emptiness.

q: Why is "Ramparts" an especially meaningful word choice for Anne’s yellow hair in stanza 1?
o: It means her hair felt as hard as brick
Like fortress walls, her dazzling outer hair blocks young men’s sight from ever reaching her real inner self behind it
It shows she guarded a literal castle
It suggests she never combed her hair
e: Just as ramparts surround a fort and block entry, her golden hair keeps suitors fixated on the surface, shielding her true inner worth.

q: Which structural device carries the sentence smoothly from line 1 to line 6 without end-punctuation in stanza 3 of "For Anne Gregory"?
o: Oxymoron
Caesura
Enjambment (sentence running across lines without terminal punctuation)
Onomatopoeia
e: When a grammatical clause continues uninterrupted from one line to the next without punctuation, it is Enjambment.

q: What does "procure" mean in "the girl in her joy promised to procure it"?
o: To scatter in a field
To forget completely
To cook thoroughly
To obtain or get hold of (especially with some effort)
e: "Procure" means to obtain or acquire something, often through effort.

q: What can you infer from the word "heretofore" in "the Prince, heretofore shielded from the sufferings of the world"?
o: That up until that exact turning point at twenty-five, royal life had completely insulated him from worldly misery
That he disliked Hindu scriptures
That he had seen poverty since birth
That he always preferred hunting
e: "Heretofore" means "until now/before that time," emphasising his sheltered palace upbringing prior to age twenty-five.

q: What does "most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges" mean?
o: Shipbuilding docks
Sacred bathing ghats where pilgrims dip in the holy river
Deep whirlpools dangerous to swimmers
Dyeing workshops for clothes
e: "Dipping places" refers to sacred river ghats where pilgrims take holy ritual dips.

q: What essential property of human existence does the potter’s earthen-vessel comparison underline?
o: Skill required in pottery
Physical immortality
Inherent fragility and the unavoidable certainty of dissolution/death
Superiority of clay over gold
e: Just as clay pots carry fragility from the moment they are shaped, human life inherently ends in mortality.

q: What does "a text" refer to in "That he had found a text to prove / That only God, my dear..."?
o: An article in an Irish newspaper
A romantic poem by a young suitor
A casual handwritten note
An authoritative passage from a sacred scripture or religious book
e: In context with "old religious man," "a text" refers to an authoritative scriptural passage.

q: What relationship between the speaker and Anne Gregory is suggested by the phrase "my dear" in the third stanza?
o: Warm, affectionate familiarity—likely an older mentor, friend, or caring poet
Cold professional distance
Complete strangers
Hostile rivalry
e: Addressing her affectionately as "my dear" conveys warm, gentle guidance rather than romantic desperation.

q: How does the principle "Not from weeping nor from grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind" apply practically to coping with personal loss?
o: Repressing all feelings forever
Moving from self-destructive despair toward acceptance, inner composure, and emotional resilience
Avoiding human relationships altogether
Blaming doctors and neighbours
e: Practically, it guides people away from self-harming wallowing toward calm acceptance and psychological composure.

q: What trait of Anne Gregory’s personality comes through in her reply ("But I can get a hair-dye...")?
o: She believes God prefers carrot hair
She hates her hair and lacks confidence
She is perceptive, spirited, and genuinely wishes to be valued for her inner character rather than shallow looks
She wants to open a beauty parlour
e: Her sharp reply reveals self-awareness and desire to be cherished for who she is inside rather than superficial charm.

q: Why do the townspeople tell Kisa Gotami, "Alas! the living are few, but the dead are many"?
o: Because they wished to refuse her mustard-seed
Because most citizens had moved away
Because a war broke out that morning
Because across generations every family has mourned loved ones; those who have passed far outnumber the living at any moment
e: It states a universal human truth: across generations, every family counts many departed loved ones compared to the living.

q: Which pedagogical technique did the Buddha use with Kisa Gotami?
o: Rote memorisation
Experiential / discovery learning, allowing her to arrive at insight firsthand
Competitive debates
Threat and punishment
e: Rather than lecturing prematurely, he designed a real-world quest so she would uncover the truth independently.

q: What does Anne’s casual list "Brown, or black, or carrot" add to the style of the poem?
o: Heavy tragic gloom
Colloquial vividness, playful wit, and youthful defiance against shallow standards
Scientific chemistry details
Monotonous repetition
e: Choosing an everyday humorous colour like "carrot" alongside "brown" and "black" adds crisp conversational wit and spirit.

q: In the sermon’s conclusion, what state does "be blessed" signify?
o: Receiving gifts from neighbours
Receiving royal treasure
Attaining profound spiritual serenity and inner grace beyond grief
Becoming a wealthy merchant
e: Here, "be blessed" denotes attaining true spiritual fulfilment and serenity after rising above grief.

q: What does the adjective "great" add to "honey-coloured / Ramparts at your ear"?
o: Short cropped length
Faded grey tone
Ugliness and neglect
Imposing visual splendour and commanding allure, reinforcing the fortress-wall image
e: Paired with "ramparts," "great" emphasises how overwhelming and visually commanding her golden hair appears.

q: In Kisa Gotami’s realization, what unlocks the "path that leads him to immortality"?
o: Surrendering all selfishness ("who has surrendered all selfishness")
Sleeping under a banyan tree for fifty years
Building stone monuments
Accumulating vast wealth
e: She directly notes that the path to immortality opens for one "who has surrendered all selfishness."

q: What emotion or awareness does the image "like an ox that is led to the slaughter" evoke?
o: Comic amusement
Solemn awareness of human helplessness before inevitable mortality
Excitement for a village fair
Pride in physical strength
e: The stark image confronts readers with sober helplessness: no human power or plea can halt the march toward death.

q: By contrasting young men’s reaction with God’s in "For Anne Gregory", what distinction is drawn about love?
o: Neither values inner goodness
God loves hair-dye better
Human attraction is easily swayed by external appearance (conditional), whereas divine love is unconditional and pure
Young men love souls more than God does

All dye their hair brown or carrot
e: Just as others judged Valli by age, young men reduce Anne to "yellow hair"; both yearn to be recognised for who they truly are inside.

q: Why does Betty Renshaw’s adaptation of "The Sermon at Benares" use formal, archaic cadence ("Alas!", "thee", "repaired to", "mark!")?
o: To create comedic confusion like Ogden Nash
Because the text was written as a casual diary
The slightly archaic, solemn cadence evokes timeless scriptural gravity and preserves the dignity of an ancient spiritual sermon
Because modern English lacked words for death
e: Formal, slightly archaic diction gives the prose the timeless resonance of sacred scripture.

q: Notice how Yeats combines "honey-coloured" (sweetness/warmth) with "Ramparts" (fortress walls): what effect does this pairing create?
o: It implies castles in Ireland were coated in honey
It warns that bees lived near Anne’s house
It suggests Anne hated sweet food
It vividly captures how sweet, dazzling beauty itself acts as a defensive barrier preventing others from seeing the real soul inside
e: Blending sweet allure ("honey-coloured") with an impenetrable barrier ("ramparts") brilliantly captures how beauty hides the inner person.

q: What drove Prince Siddhartha to renounce wealth, palace life, and royal status at age twenty-five?
o: Ambition for a larger kingdom
Deep compassion stirred by seeing human suffering (sickness, age, death) and an urgent quest to understand and transcend it
Dispute with his royal teachers
Desire for tourist adventures
e: It was selfless compassion: despite enjoying total personal comfort, witnessing universal suffering drove him to seek wisdom for all.

q: At the end of Kisa Gotami’s roadside vigil, literal night darkness reigns—yet what metaphorical light dawns inside her?
o: A fire in a nearby pottery shop
The inner light of wisdom and selflessness that dispels her blindness of ego and futile grief
A lantern carried by a passing soldier
Sunrise occurring an hour later
e: Even as outer city lights go out into darkness, the inner illumination of wisdom awakens within her.

q: If Anne Gregory responded thoughtfully after hearing the lesson of "The Sermon at Benares", which attitude would best align both texts?
o: That mustard-seed dyes hair naturally
That outer looks guarantee peace of mind
That physical beauty, like mortal youth, is fleeting and superficial, whereas inner selflessness and spiritual truth endure
That everyone should chase yellow hair forever
e: Both texts invite us to look beyond transient externals—whether futile attachment to mortal form or superficial beauty—toward enduring spiritual truth.

q: Why do readers feel deep empathy rather than judgement toward Kisa Gotami, even though she initially behaves irrationally?
o: Because she was very wealthy
Because the neighbours lied to her
Because she travelled from far away
Because a mother’s desperate refusal to lose her only child springs from pure love and raw grief; the story treats her gently, guiding her from pain to wisdom
e: Her frantic denial stems from immense maternal love; neither the Buddha nor the narrative mocks her, instead guiding her gently toward peace.

q: How does invoking God’s unconditional love at the close of "For Anne Gregory" elevate the whole poem?
o: It elevates a playful debate about hair-dye and flirting into a philosophical meditation on the rarity of pure, unconditional love
It turns the poem into a horror story
It forbids young people from dating
It insults the old religious man
e: Beginning as witty banter about hair colour, stanza 3 lifts the poem into a gentle meditation on human fragility versus divine love.

q: According to the Buddha’s teaching, how can you recognise someone who has truly found "peace of mind"?
o: They refuse all water and rest
They stay composed, free from bitter complaint and selfish lamentation, living calmly beyond grief
They collect mustard-seeds across villages
They judge mourning neighbours harshly
e: Peace manifests as emotional composure—freedom from bitterness, self-pity, and destructive grief.

q: Compare Siddhartha sitting under the peepal tree for seven days with Kisa Gotami sitting by the wayside at night—what symbolic parallel unites them?
o: Both scenes take place during noisy markets
Both characters fell asleep without thinking
Both experienced a quiet moment of stillness and direct observation away from frantic action, leading to life-changing spiritual awakening
Both were built inside royal palaces
e: In both cases, stopping frantic pursuit to sit in quiet observation unlocks profound truth.

q: Synthesising both the prose and poem of Chapter 8, what twin wisdom can a student carry into real life?
o: Move permanently to Benares and dye hair carrot-red
Avoid all friendships and buy only earthen pots
Judge people by clothing and mourn loudly
Accept mortality to overcome selfish grief with inner composure, and value inner worth over superficial outer appearances
e: Together they teach deep emotional maturity: accepting life’s impermanence peacefully while looking past shallow exteriors to true inner worth.
